title: Justified by faith
hook: Protestants stress being declared right with God by faith in Christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, a real body raised: broiled fish, scarred hands, a body, not a ghost. What did your own hands tell you? Day one thousand eighty-eight.

Night, and a man with no children. In Genesis, God brings Abram outside and says: look up. "Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them." So shall your descendants be. Abram has nothing to show for this promise. No baby, no plan, no proof. Just the sky. And then comes a single sentence in Genesis that Paul will later build a whole argument on: "And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness." In this scene he does nothing but trust. And it was counted. Today's word: justification.

To justify, in Paul's letters, is a courtroom word. It means a judge declaring someone in the right. Not making excuses for them. Pronouncing a verdict. Here's the startling line in Romans: God is the one "that justifieth the ungodly." Not the good. The ungodly. And how? In Paul's words, "his faith is counted for righteousness," exactly like Abram under the stars. So Paul writes, "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." The verdict comes first, and peace follows. For the Protestant Reformers, this was the heart of it. Martin Luther said he had been terrified of a God who judges, until he read Romans and saw that the righteousness of God was something given, not something demanded. The Reformers' phrase was faith alone. And Ephesians puts it plainly: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Now the honest part. James, in the same Bible, says: "Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only." Protestants read James as describing living faith, the kind that can't help showing up in what you do. Catholics teach that God's justifying grace both declares and truly makes a person righteous, with faith working through love, as Paul says to the Galatians. Lutheran and Catholic leaders have signed a joint declaration saying they share a basic understanding of justification, while still differing on details. Tomorrow, an Orthodox picture of salvation. Today's picture is a courtroom, and a verdict nobody earned.

Here's the practice: receive one thing as a gift. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something good in your life you didn't earn: a person who loves you, a morning, a talent, a second chance. Notice the urge to explain why you deserve it, or to pay it back right away. Let that urge go quiet. Just receive it, the way Abram looked at the sky with nothing in his hands. If you pray, you can thank God for it. If you don't, just say thank you, to no one in particular. The bell holds the time.
Justification. Being declared right with God, a verdict that Protestants stress is received by faith in Christ, as a gift.
Your line: declared right. Today, when someone thanks you or praises you, don't argue. Just say thank you, and let it land. Day one thousand eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Lutheran, Reformed and evangelical churches preach justification by grace through faith as the heart of the gospel, and Lutherans and some other Protestants mark Reformation Day each year; Catholic teaching speaks of justification as a gift of grace that also makes a person righteous.

pairs: it is the gift of God

myth: in Romans, God justifies the good
Paul says God "justifieth the ungodly." the verdict is a gift.
James says a man is justified by works, and not by faith only
Protestants read it as living faith showing itself; Catholics read it with faith working through love.
Lutheran and Catholic leaders have never agreed on anything about justification
they have signed a joint declaration on a basic shared understanding, while still differing on details.

fork.setup: you're Abram. you have no children. God says, look at the stars: so shall your descendants be. what does Genesis say you do?
fork.reveal: "and he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness." Paul builds his argument in Romans on this one line.

original.note: Greek: justification, a declaring right. Romans 4:25: raised again for our justification.

trapdoor: what you thought: justifying means making excuses.
what it means: a verdict. God declaring someone right, and in Paul it is received by faith, as a gift.
what a scholar hears: Romans 4 rests on Genesis 15:6. and James answers "not by faith only," which the churches read in different ways.

notes: Romans 4:5 is quoted in two pieces in the voice ('that justifieth the ungodly' and 'His faith is counted for righteousness'); the source line joins them with the KJV comma. Confirm.
Luther's account of his terror and breakthrough reading Romans is from his 1545 Preface; paraphrased. Confirm.
Catholic teaching summarized (justification both declares and makes righteous; faith working through love) per Trent Session 6; confirm fairness.

Joint Declaration (Lutheran World Federation and Catholic Church, signed 1999; later affirmed by other churches): no date stated in script. Confirm 'basic understanding' phrasing ('a consensus in basic truths').
Original δικαίωσις appears in Romans 4:25 and 5:18; confirm pronunciation.

Editor pass: Genesis 15 gives no age and no tent, so the hook, its screen head and the fork no longer call Abram 'old' or place him 'outside his tent'; he is a childless man God brings outside (15:2–5).
Audit pass (2026-10-02): 'He didn't do anything' stated one reading as fact in the narrator's voice (James 2:21-23 reads Abraham's faith through his deeds); narrowed to 'in this scene'.
